# Draft:Leopoldina von Schwarzenberg-Hohenlansberg

Leopoldina-Augusta, Countess of Schwarzenberg-Hohenlansberg (born Princess Leopoldina of Reuss-Köstritz; 8 August 1840 — 5 December 1926), was a German courtier, writer, and collector, best remembered for her service as a lady-in-waiting to Empress Augusta of Germany during the heightened period of the German Empire. A member of the cadet branch of the House of Reuss, she married into the prominent Schwarzenberg-Hohenlansberg family, whose other branches held considerable influence in Austria-Hungary. Known in her lifetime for her cultural salons in Berlin, and later in Vienna following the First World War, she was a notable figure in imperial court life and the intellectual circles of fin-de-siècle Central Europe.
Early Adolescence
Leopoldina-Augusta von Schwarzenberg-Hohenlansberg (née Reuss-Köstritz) was born on August 8th, 1840, within the confines of the Schloss Ebersdorf, in present-day Thuringia, then known as the Principality of Reuss-Erbersdorf. She was the eighth child and youngest daughter of Prince Heinrich LXIII of Reuss-Köstritz through his second marriage to Countess Caroline of Stolberg-Wernigerode. Her adolescence consisted of a relatively domestic lifestyle in the countryside, primarily at the Schloss Köstritz near Gera. There, she was tutored under the guise of a governess in Geography and Literature: to name a few of the educational standards at the time for someone of her rank. In her spare time, Leopoldina often accompanied her mother on carriage rides through sparse villages near the Schloss, where she was taught from an early age, acts of charity to those less fortunate than herself. She also developed a fondness for watercolor, most of her early works depicting landscapes. As was fashionable at the time, she constantly switched between two residences during her youth: the Schloss Scharfenberg in Klipphausen during the summer, with its abundance of fishing and hunting land, and her childhood home for the remainder of the year. It wouldn’t be until 1857, at the age of seventeen, that Leopoldina, at the request of her mother, would spend the winter in Berlin, where the Prussian social season often sequestered itself. The same year, she was presented to Emperor Wilhelm I and his consort at the Schloss Berlin during an event, marking her entry into aristocratic German society.
Marriage and Court Life
The next year, on October 22nd, 1858, Leopoldina married Count Georg von Schwarzenberg-Hohenlansberg, a member of a cadet branch of the House of Schwarzenberg, one of the most prominent lineages of the Habsburg monarchy. The aforementioned line had been established in the 15th century, and carried both Prussian and Frisian origins. Although not as politically influential as the princely main line, the cadet branch controlled large estates in Lower Austria and in the Dutch-speaking states. Leading up to the marriage, negotiations were briefly halted over the concern over religion, as Leopoldina had been raised as a Protestant, and her future husband as a Catholic. It appears that this had not been too much of an issue, as the couple married with much local fanfare at the Wallfahrtskirche Maria Geburt in Scheinfeld, at the request of the Schwarzenberg-Hohenlansberg family. Leading up to the ceremony, Leopoldina dutifully converted to Catholicism in a private ceremony. She thus began her life as a married, provincial noble. The couple began an extensive honeymoon a few days later, first staying with relatives and close acquaintances at various country seats before crossing the Austrian border to stay at the extensive Schwarzenberg properties. Such included a brief respite at the Schloss Frauenberg in Lower Bohemia, with an additional stop in Prague, of which Leopoldina grew fond. Following this, the couple resided primarily at the Schloss Schwarzenberg in Scheinfeld, but later acquired the Schloss Seehaus as a quant summer property. The couple socialized primarily with the Bavarian court; however, due to the Dutch connotations with their title, occasionally spent time at the Belgian court as well. During this period of relative domesticity, Leopoldina carried out extensive redecorating of both properties. In 1865, she would give birth to a son, Heinrich-Georg, and a year later, to another son, Wilhelm, to the joy of her extended family.
Leopoldina continued to live in a provincial setting, although a leading figure in the region. In 1860, she would be selected as a lady-in-waiting to Marie of Prussia, Queen of Bavaria. Occasionally, she would also designate some time to travel to Berlin, but these trips were far and few between. In 1891, Leopoldina was appointed as a lady-in-waiting to Empress Augusta of Schleswig-Holstein, which solidified a semi-permanent move to Berlin. Having been recommended favorably by the Bavarian monarchs, Leopoldina was selected to assist in organizing ceremonial events on behalf of the Empress, as well as to support the preparation of court ceremonies. Her ascension to a court position enabled her to become a recipient of the femable Order of Louise, which she received a year later, in 1892. Additionally, Leopoldina was given the option of grace-and-favor apartments within the Schloss Berlin, but coupled with her husband’s hereditary appointment as a senior court marshal to the German Emperor, the couple instead decided to purchase a neoclassical residence within the perimeters of the Tiergarten. As a gift, partial funding from the monarchs to purchase the residence was given to the couple. The establishment of a private home in Berlin thrust Leopoldina into a golden age of societal favoritism. She was quick to establish a salon, having surrounded herself with Berlin’s most notable aristocrats. Her salon was frequented not only by elites but by intellectuals as well; foreign diplomats and members of the various political parties, among some of the prominent invitees, which allowed her to make extensive connections across Europe. Leopoldina was one of the few aristocrats to embrace political discussions within her salon, and instead, it became a flourishing of cultural and reformist exchange. Her worldview simultaneously widened when she accompanied the Empress on an official tour to the Ottoman Empire in 1898. Following the tour, she gained an interest in collecting, and soon procured massive installments of antique furniture and artworks from auction houses, which she used to decorate many of the Schwarzenberg-Hohenlansberg properties.
Self-Imposed Exile and Later Years
In 1914, Leopoldina had planned to visit the Austrian Archduke Franz Ferdinand and his wife, the Duchess of Hohenberg, at their Bohemian estate. This never happened following their assassination. Leopoldina wrote in her private memoirs that she felt a sense of unease following the event, hoping to come out unscathed from any conflict that might arise as a result. The relatively early years of the war were quite tranquil. Leopoldina contributed to various charities to support the war effort and even opened a wing of her Berlin residence to be used as a small clinic. Following in the footsteps of many aristocratic women at the time, she trained with the German Red Cross, but largely consigned herself to administrative work for the organization instead of nursing. As the war took a dismal turn, her husband served under the Bavarian Cuirassiers and, on August 12th, 1918, died at the Battle of Amiens. That same day, Leopoldina received news of his death via an expedited message to Berlin. As a result, she plunged into mourning. Her two sons also served within the same division, but survived the war. As political tensions were beginning to fray and the monarchy started to lose its grip on its subjects, Leopoldina was directed by the German Empress to leave for her country estate to avoid the turmoil occurring in Berlin. She refused on account of her duties as a lady-in-waiting and made plans to join the monarchs at Spa, in Belgium, where they were headquartered. Due to threats against her person, as an aristocrat, she had to change her plans and instead headed for the Austrian border, where she was assured by her in-laws that she would be placed under their care. On October 16th, she left Berlin, never to see it again. After a quick stop at her properties in the country, she arrived in Vienna six days later. Upon arrival there, she received news that during her travels, her Berlin residence had been ransacked and converted to headquarters for the emerging provisional government. Thus, was a symbol that her life in Germany was no longer.
Following the collapse of the German and Austrian monarchy, Leopoldina realized that her title no longer held the same connotations it had before the war. However, she was still referred to by her title in upper-class social circles of post-war Vienna. She stayed there only through the winter of 1918, and in the new year, relocated to the newly established Czechoslovak Republic, settling in the Schloss Fraunenberg. She lived there until her death on December 7th, 1921. She was later interned at the Schwarzeberg crypt alongside her husband in Třeboň.
